    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    In Graphic Detail: The GTA 6 creator industrial complex

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • The most anticipated modern video game, Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), was released a week ago today, selling $3.79 billion in just a single day of sales.
    • According to analytics website Stream Charts, GTA 6 beat every other major game’s full-week watch time in just two days, and did so with ease, hitting 214.6 million hours watched in two days, versus the next highest game, Valorant’s 150.48 million hours in a week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    The most anticipated modern video game, Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), was released a week ago today, selling $3.79 billion in just a single day of sales. Creators have been preparing for GTA 6’s release for years, figuring out ways to stand out from the millions playing the game and the thousands of people making content around it.

    According to analytics website Stream Charts, GTA 6 beat every other major game’s full-week watch time in just two days, and did so with ease, hitting 214.6 million hours watched in two days, versus the next highest game, Valorant’s 150.48 million hours in a week.

    “A record was never in doubt. Rockstar’s gameplay reveal in August already drew close to 4 million concurrent viewers, for a game nobody could play yet,” Streams Charts product manager Nazar Babenko told Digiday.

    Sources indicate that A week later, let’s take a look at how the GTA 6 creator economy over the last week (and the months leading up to it), including the livestream watch hours, the most popular platforms, the top streamers, and the organic cultural conversation around the game. Just how major is GTA 6? Unsurprisingly: Huge.

    Industry observers note that ahead of GTA 6’s launch, platforms saw a marked increase in content around the franchise and the previous game, GTA 5, which launched in 2013. Streamlabs reports that GTA 5’s year-to-date viewership was higher than several other major, more current video games.

    Streams Chart’s seven-day GTA 6 numbers showcase the game generated more watch time on Twitch alone than any previous game launch had across all platforms the manufacturer tracks.

    “Hours watched surprised us more than the peak,” remarked Babenko.

    Creators who built a name and audience for themselves making GTA 5 content have been preparing for GTA 6 for over a year (the game release, initially slated for November 2025, was delayed twice, and the game was officially unveiled in 2023).

    According to recent reports, reed Duchscher, CEO and founder of talent agency Night Media, remarked that GTA creator Andre “Typical Gamer” Rebelo (who has 16.3 million followers on YouTube), has perfected his video-on-demand content (VOD) with GTA 5 and was prepared for GTA 6. “He’ll have a bunch of video concepts that he’ll go film away from his livestream and then post on YouTube because most people will be so concerned about beating the campaign,” Duchscher said. “He has a wealth of knowledge from GTA 5 and a huge catalog on YouTube, so we know what video concepts are going to do well.”.

    According to Streams Charts, there were over 125 million hours watched of GTA 6 gameplay in just 24 hours (November 18 to November 19). Twitch drove the most views, accounting for 1.7% of views (market intelligence firm Sensor Tower reports Twitch mobile app downloads and daily active consumers increased by more than 80% day over day on those two days), then YouTube, which pulled in 35.1%. Kick came in third with 22.1%, while other live streaming platforms made up the difference – which was still over 1.3 million hours of watch time.

    It has been revealed that notably, YouTube organized a 24-hour livestream with some of its top creators, but was still beaten by Twitch, possibly because the platform announced during TwitchCon 2026 that it would be giving away copies of the game through surprise daily drops. Both Twitch and YouTube added custom GTA 6 badges, animations, and effects.

    In a recent development, though Twitch edged out YouTube for livestream watch hours in the first day of GTA 6’s launch, YouTube still saw over 3.5 billion global views of videos with GTA 6 in the title the day of release. To date, YouTube reports the Grand Theft Auto series has over 900 billion views, and that GTA 6 videos hit 40 billion views before November 18.

    In a recent development, within the first week since launch, there have been 420 million hours watched of GTA 6 across all major platforms, with peak viewers hitting 7.91 million. Stream Charts reports the game has been mentioned in livestream chats over 3.2 million times across more than 55,000 channels, with sentiment almost split between positive and negative – that could be largely attributed to the online reactionary response to some gameplay elements that involve fixing up a nice and being nice to your girlfriend.

    Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, perhaps the biggest streamer in the world, Darren Jason “IShowSpeed” Watkins Jr., drew the most eyes during the first 24 hours post-release, with 4.7 million watch hours across YouTube and Twitch. Close behind him was a streamer known as The Burnt Peanut, with 3.8 million watch hours across YouTube, Twitch and Kick.

    In third was Brazilian streamer Alan “Alanzoka” Ferreira, who notably generated 3.1 million hours watched during launch day solely on Twitch.

    It has been revealed that in just a week, GTA 6 has edged out some of the most popular streaming categories and video games, drawing more views than Kick’s entire IRL stream category, and drawing close to its Just Chatting category. As of halfway through 2026, Just Chatting had become the most-watched category across all major streaming platforms, signaling that they were shifting from gaming-focused content to more IRL and commentary content. But GTA 6 appears to have shifted the livestream platforms back to what they were first made for: Gaming.

    Recent findings suggest that A broad “gaming” category is the most-watched on all of YouTube within the last month, and the fourth-most watched on Twitch. Even GTA 5, the previous installment in the franchise, ranked in the top ten most-watched categories over the last 30 days. Gaming is back, and creators will likely lean further into its popularity, especially those who don’t typical game.

    It has been revealed that according to Streams Charts, 1,056 channels reached a new all-time peak viewership record while streaming GTA 6, with the most records held by YouTube creators. According to the week after launch report, almost one in five record-breaking channels received at least ten times as many concurrent viewers as their pre-GTA 6 peak.

    According to recent reports, according to data pulled by influencer marketing agency Linqia, the GTA 6 hype was almost entirely organic. Its creator data pulled during the pre-launch GTA 6 period (April 1 through November 18), indicates that 97.8 percent of creators posting about GTA 6 were doing so organically, with just 2.2 percent sponsored. Rockstar Games did not pay a single creator who took part in Linqia’s study, while 7 percent of the paid creators came from prediction market Kalshi – notably not a gaming brand.

    “The most active brands were the platforms,” stated Babenko. Two-thirds of creators talking about GTA 6 never even mentioned a brand. According to Linqia, it seems sponsorships might actually hurt content performance: sponsored posts that name-dropped GTA 6 performed 3 percent worse than each creator’s typical sponsored post. You can’t fake the GTA 6 hype.

    Industry observers note that “I think a lot of brands leaned in from an organic social standpoint but many outside of gaming didn’t think creator first for GTA,” remarked Keith Bendes, chief strategy officer at Liniqia. “Which was a substantial missed opportunity since creators were clearly talking organically about the game in droves.”.

    The creator economy is shifting its stance on clipping as platforms crackdown; what does clipping look like in the future?

    OpenAI revised its ChatGPT Business Hub terms following concerns that the original language could restrict businesses’ legal claims.

    Grand Theft Auto 6 has its own content creator cottage industry, with millions of views and a crowded, competitive marketplace.

    Tech Report: Dick’s Sporting Goods is turning youth sports into a premium ad business

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • Dick’s Sporting Goods has found that there’s significant business in youth sports.
    • The sporting retailer recorded a third quarter GAAP net income of $161 million in earnings this week — more than double the $75 million reported the year prior.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Dick’s Sporting Goods has found that there’s significant business in youth sports.

    The sporting retailer recorded a third quarter GAAP net income of $161 million in earnings this week — more than double the $75 million reported the year prior.

    Dick’s execs attributed much of that success to Dick’s Media Network, home to its youth sports app GameChange.

    According to recent reports, like many long-tail retail media networks, Dick’s Sporting Goods doesn’t break out its ad business revenue by dollar figure or percentage. Dick’s chief financial officer Navdeep Gupta noted that the manufacturer is grappling with supply-chain related costs, higher fuel costs and other pressures, but Dick’s Media Network partially offset those pressures.

    “We have talked about these gross margin growth drivers with Dick’s Media Network and GameChanger. Those are continuing to be very differentiated drivers of not only our profitability, but our gross margin expansion,” he mentioned.

    Sources indicate that dick’s Media Network is four years old and offers ad units in-store, on its own site, off-site across the open web, social and streaming. Perhaps its biggest get is its live sports via GameChanger.

    According to recent reports, “They found this gap in the marketplace in terms of sports club video streaming. And they’ve created this app, this solution, and now they inherently have their own O&O [owned and operated] inventory from a media perspective,” mentioned Olivia Hawkins, vp of media strategy at Salt XC.

    It has been revealed that dick’s has previously worked with sports brands like Adidas, On, Under Armor and Crocs. However, the sports retailer is actively engaging non-endemic partners too.

    Sources indicate that take Chobani, for example. The yogurt brand bought ad space on Dick’s Sporting Goods Game Changer app during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, noted Hawkins, who was familiar with the deal.

    Industry observers note that she did not disclose financial details of the ad buy. The campaign focused on reach and awareness, getting Chobani in front of youth sports enthusiasts, like parents and coaches, Hawkins mentioned.

    “They met our expectations in terms of reaching a fresh audience and delivery, frequency, and all those media metrics — CPM and video completions and all that,” she noted, without detailing the campaign’s success.

    Dick’s video app CPMs are more premium, hovering around $35, according to one commerce executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

    Industry observers note that “That’s more expensive than significant TV. They’re asking for that price for that type of inventory. It’s a great solution — super clever, but it’s expensive,” the anonymous exec told Digiday. In comparison, Netflix CPMs fell from their initial $60 when it launched in 2022 to the low $20s at the moment.

    It has been revealed that seemingly, brands are willing to cough up the dough. That’s the bet Dick’s seems to be making. It makes sense given sports has become the industry’s latest golden goose.

    Put some numbers on it. In a survey this year, Dick’s Media and eMarketer reported that 63% of U.S. parents have kids in youth sports and 84% of them stated youth sports influence their buying choices.

    Now, there’s the question of scale. Dick’s GameChanger app has more than 5 million monthly active users, but youth sports is more niche than something like the National Football League, which averages 18.7 million viewers per game during the regular season.

    “It’s a great audience. It’s a great inventory, but it is finite versus other offsite environments that include all of the open web,” Hawkins said.

    That leaves Dick’s in the same boat as other retail media networks — or at least every other RMN that isn’t Amazon or Walmart — where continued growth may have to come from beyond retailers’ owned and operated channels.

    #215623. Brands race to systematize how to know what makes creator content worth paying for

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (906 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Brands race to systematize how to know what makes creator content worth paying for

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • Social media trends move faster than brands can keep up with.
    • Home to brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Trix, the CPG brand has spent the past year putting together an internal framework to systematize monetizing viral moments.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Social media trends move faster than brands can keep up with. Now, they’re trying to create repeatable systems to turn organic social attention into something they can evaluate, fund and ultimately scale.

    Take General Mills, for example. Home to brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Trix, the CPG brand has spent the past year putting together an internal framework to systematize monetizing viral moments.

    Its “talkability score” is a calculation used to measure whether General Mills’ brands are earning more attention with social media creators than they’re buying with paid ads. It’s a loose framework that varies by brand, Mindy Murray, director of influencer and content at General Mills said, and generates a score based on whether consumers shared it, put their own spin on it and how long interest in the trend lasts.

    Industry observers note that murray was mum on the actual mechanics on how it actually determines whether to invest ad spend. “We’re weighing on earning, we’re weighing things like active engagement — so shares likes, comments, saves — because we know that that means someone took an actual effort to do something versus just an impression,” Murray said.

    Virality can’t be manufactured, but this “operating system” allows them to “go faster and be smarter,” noted Murray.

    Over the past year, General Mills has also reorganized its teams to bring social and influencer marketing under Murray’s purview, she told Digiday, to move more rapidly and efficiently in converting buzzy organic content into paid ads.

    For example, over the summer Reese’s “Eat ‘Em Up” cereal jingle from the early 2000s started trending on TikTok. General Mills noticed the trend, partnered with GloRilla to re-record the rap, tracked real-time activity via its framework, and ultimately turned it into a campaign on streaming platforms and Reese’s Puffs’ YouTube channel. The manufacturer boasted a 2.5% year-over-year sales increase as a result, but did not provide specific sales figures. The company did not say specifically how the framework informed that strategy.

    Last week, influencer agency Billion Dollar Boy (BDB) rolled out its Creator Investment Planner, a financial modeling tool that aims to help marketers understand the ad spend levels required to plan and “de-risk creator investments,” according to a news release.

    In a recent development, BDB’s tool works by calculating blended CPMs from creators and social media platforms. Marketers enter their budget and time frame, and the platform calculates estimates for share of voice, total impressions and earned media value. Per BDB, the model can revision as inputs change, where marketers can expect to “de-risk” spend commitments.

    In a recent development, and in April, CreatorIQ creator platform and creative analytics and governance platform CreativeX rolled out a fresh tool to help brands incorporate creator content into a paid media strategy. The system works on an API, sending creator content from CreatorIQ’s platform to CreativeX to be graded, reviewed by CreativeX’s AI-powered system and optimized by a brand campaign manager. Ultimately, it aims to identify creator posts with potential to do well as an ad before any media buyers open their wallets. Nestlé was the first brand to sign on. The integration was declared on an invite-only basis.

    To agency execs, all signs point to brands getting more rigorous about their spend — especially when it comes to squeezing performance out of creators — and do it before the trend disappears.

    Sources indicate that creator spend is expected to increase 12% every year until 2030, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall. In no small part, brand spend on boosting or promoting creator content is fueling that growth.

    “Before any sort of budget is unlocked, you have to be able to prove out that there’s a higher propensity for that piece of content for whatever investment you’re making into social to actually move towards a conversion,” said Madison Gaudry-Routledge, evp of social at Viral Nation, a social agency.

    Most brands, Gaudry-Routledge said, haven’t come up with a named framework in the same way General Mills has. Brand spend on creator marketing is expected to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising. Naturally, brands are eager to see proof of concept as early as possible.

    Industry observers note that viral Nation has its own proprietary framework offered to clients as an add-on service. It’s called Culture Quotient that blends brand awareness, brand affinity and brand velocity into a measurable score to determine a brand’s relevance in cultural conversation. The tool works via AI that analyzes conversations and content, identifies emerging cultural trends and tracks shifts in consumer sentiment, per Gaudry-Routledge. The social exec declined to share any client-specific examples.

    These calculations are being built in real time and haven’t yet replaced traditional metrics like share of voice, audience sentiment and engagement.

    “As an industry, we’re continuing to try to catch up on operationalizing frameworks and systematizing measurement and still not there yet,” remarked Kristina Coughlin, svp and general manager of Trevant, a creator marketing agency.

    Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring newly introduced customers this holiday season.

    Product discovery habits are changing, leaving marketers unsure how to pivot ahead of the biggest sales period of the year.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI can raise the ceiling on marketing, or it can expose every weak foundation underneath it.
    • Live from the Marketing Vanguard stage at Brandweek 2026, Jenny Rooney sits down with Laura Knebusch, senior vice president of CPG marketing and customer experience at Georgia-Pacific, to explore what modern brand building really requires when media, data, retail, and AI are all evolving at once.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI can raise the ceiling on marketing, or it can expose every weak foundation underneath it.

    Live from the Marketing Vanguard stage at Brandweek 2026, Jenny Rooney sits down with Laura Knebusch, senior vice president of CPG marketing and customer experience at Georgia-Pacific, to explore what modern brand building really requires when media, data, retail, and AI are all evolving at once.

    Laura gets into why Georgia-Pacific spent 18 months consolidating data sources, and how that foundation now supports in-house capabilities and agentic AI.

    She also discusses why consumer-first and AI-first marketing are not actually competing ideas.

    This episode is part of a special vidcast series that was recorded live during Brandweek 2026 and presented in partnership with Tatari.

    Laura Knebusch is Senior Vice President of CPG Marketing and Customer Experience at Georgia-Pacific, where her team supports consumer and B2B brands across insights, content, media, promotions, marketing technology and analytics.

    She began her marketing career at Procter & Gamble after earning her MBA from Duke and later joined Georgia-Pacific, where she has spent 18 years across brand management, category leadership and marketing capability roles.

    Today, her focus is on combining classic brand-building fundamentals with the data, technology and operating models needed for modern CPG marketing.

    It has been revealed that private Label Is Waiting, So What About Your Brand? — Laura points out that consumers have been adjusting their behavior for years, not reacting to one sudden economic moment. In household essentials, private-label options are credible and easy to access. There’s a warning lying there for marketers: if the brand does not create a real reason to choose it, loyalty becomes much harder to defend.

    Sources indicate that 100 Data Sources, One Source of Truth, Eighteen Months of Work — When Laura stepped into her current role, Georgia-Pacific needed to become more digitally capable. The first step was not another tool. It was fixing the data. Over 18 months, the team connected roughly 100 different sources, cleaned and harmonized them, and built one accessible system that now powers multiple in-house capabilities.

    In a recent development, consumer-First vs. AI-First Is the Wrong Debate — At Brandweek 2026, Laura describes an internal discussion that paired behavioral science with generative-engine optimization. At first, the advice sounded different – Humans need simplicity, distinctiveness and repetition, while AI needs clear, consistent information. But the conclusion was the same: strong fundamentals work for both.

    In a recent development, why Georgia-Pacific Merged Shopper Marketing and National Media — Retail media has changed how consumers discover and buy, so Georgia-Pacific changed how it organizes around that reality. Laura explains why shopper marketing and national media were brought closer together, helping the team better understand where partners create strategic value and where investment should stay tactical.

    Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

    #215590. Latest Update: Want to Sell an Agency? Launch a Creator Marketing Firm

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2215 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adweek ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Want to Sell an Agency? Launch a Creator Marketing Firm

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In recent months, the market for creator and social agencies has been, to put it lightly, brisk.
    • In September, the Madrid-based social agency Samy acquired Get Engaged, a U.S.
    • In October, Billion Dollar Boy Group bought Creator Authority, a business-to-business influencer agency, and the private equity firm Shamrock Capital, which owns ADWEEK, made an eight-figure investment in the social-first agency Saylor.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In recent months, the market for creator and social agencies has been, to put it lightly, brisk.

    In September, the Madrid-based social agency Samy acquired Get Engaged, a U.S. social and influencer shop, in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

    In October, Billion Dollar Boy Group bought Creator Authority, a business-to-business influencer agency, and the private equity firm Shamrock Capital, which owns ADWEEK, made an eight-figure investment in the social-first agency Saylor.

    Sources indicate that earlier this month, the social-first agency LV8 merged with its sister firm Mirage Digital on the back of a “high eight figures” investment from Velocity Capital Management. And last week, the private equity firm Falfurrias Management Partners took a majority stake in Freeman & Forrest, another B2B creator agency.

    Industry observers note that the deals are part of a record year, according to James Creech, founder of the creator M&A advisory firm Quartermast. There have been 30 agency acquisitions in the creator economy so far in 2026, up from 20 in all of 2025 and above the previous high of 28 in 2022, according to Quartermast data.

    Overall, there have been 124 M&A creator-adjacent deals this year, the busiest on record, and roughly half of the agency deals have come since July, per Quartermast.

    Behind the surge is a crop of boutiques founded during the pandemic-era influencer boom that have matured into businesses worth buying, which are run by founders who need more resources to keep up with what clients are asking for.

    Recent findings suggest that A specific set of firms—social-first creative shops, podcast agencies, TikTok Shop specialists, and B2B creator plays—are responsible for the majority of this interest, while the deals themselves are increasingly financed by a new cohort of buyers, including private equity firms, strategic roll-ups, and international firms. All of it is unfolding in a frothy market for creator economy deals, which is just now beginning to consolidate in response to urgent demand across a fragmented space.

    Recent findings suggest that “Creator marketing works,” Creech noted. “Brands and their agency partners are going to continue to invest there.”.

    The current rush of creator agency activity has its origins in the pandemic, according to LV8 chief executive Griffin Haddrill.

    Lockdown acted as a digital accelerant, pulling budgets toward creators at a moment when television and film had dried up and out-of-home advertising had stopped working.

    Because acquisitions typically take nine to 12 months to come together, the resulting deal volume spiked in 2021 and 2022, slowed over the following two years, and has since normalized, Creech said.

    Industry observers note that the same period produced a wave of new agencies, many of which were founded by executives who saw the emerging relevance of the creator ecosystem and launched startups to service it. Five years later, those boutiques have matured into businesses worth buying, according to Haddrill.

    FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context.

    For founders, selling offers the resources to keep up with clients, according to Get Engaged co-founder Ben Hiott.

    “Social is becoming the center of how brands build their businesses, and clients are asking us to do more every year,” Hiott mentioned in October.

    The wave of dealmaking that followed the pandemic was primarily influencer agencies, according to Creech, while this year, the variety of targets has expanded.

    In 2026, buyers have gone after social-first creative agencies, such as Get Engaged, OK Cool, and Sway Social; podcast and audio shops like Ad Results Media and Listening Party Agency; and TikTok Shop specialists including Orca, Uptickk, and Yada.

    According to recent reports, private equity is also getting more involved in the space, investing capital after years of financing strategic acquirers, as Bridgepoint does with Samy, according to Creech. This year, Shamrock Capital took a majority stake in Saylor, Velocity became a near-equal partner in LV8, and Falfurrias bought Freeman & Forrest, among other deals.

    Serial acquirers are consolidating the field as well. Influencer agency Ykone has made four acquisitions in 2026, and creator company network Residence has made two, while Samy and Publicis remain active, according to Creech. After large platform deals for Influential and Captiv8, Publicis has turned to regional acquisitions, including the French creator agency Point d’Orgue, to enter fresh markets, according to Creech.

    For investors, the opportunity lies in stitching these shops together, according to Haddrill.

    Sources indicate that “The consumer demand was there, but the agency space was fragmented,” Haddrill said. “Now, investors are seeing this fragmentation and working to bring them together.”.

    B2B creator marketing has also emerged as its own category.

    Creator Authority, whose clients include Amazon, Adobe, and Mastercard, was Billion Dollar Boy Group’s first acquisition, an all-cash, multimillion-dollar deal with an earnout component, according to Business Insider.

    Freeman & Forrest, founded in 2024 by Emily Freeman and Forrest Brazeal after they ran influencer programs at Microsoft and Google Cloud, helps tech companies like Amazon and Google reach technical customers through creators.

    According to recent reports, and more of the deals cross borders: Get Engaged gave Samy a U.S. base after the agency built its business in Europe and Latin America, and dealmaking between the U.S. and the U.K. has picked up in both directions, according to Creech.

    As the ecosystem matures, the next wave of dealmaking may come from the middle of the market, according to a creator management executive who asked not to be named.

    The largest independents, such as Whalar and Influential, have already sold to Accenture Song and Publicis, respectively, which leaves room for midsize independents, many of which will come to market over the next 12 months, the executive noted.

    Creator management firms, which run creators’ businesses rather than simply booking their brand deals, are likely the next category to consolidate, the executive added.

    The buying, in other words, is far from over, according to Creech.

    “It’s mature, it’s scaled, it’s professionalized. The work is not done,” Creech said. “We’re maybe entering middle innings.”.

    Hearst CMO Heads Out (SCOOP): The chief marketing officer at Hearst Magazines, Sherri Chambers, will be leaving the organization in a few weeks, according to sources. Chambers, who joined the digital media firm in December 2024, confirmed the news, while a Hearst Magazines spokesperson expressed their gratitude for Chambers in a statement. The departure is the latest in a series of executive shake-ups. In July, Hearst Magazines appointed Chris Berend as its first chief content and experience officer, and in October, it named A+E executive Juliana Stock as its new president, replacing Debi Chirichella, who will become chair of the group. The legacy media firm has worked hard to cultivate a reputation for calm and consistency in an otherwise turbulent industry, but it certainly looks as if the firm is aiming to turn some kind of corner.

    In a recent development, bunny Boss Bolts: The editor in chief of Playboy, Phillip Picardi, has left the organization after less than a year, Puck reported earlier this week. According to a organization spokesperson, the move was a personal decision, with Picardi returning to Los Angeles after Playboy set up headquarters in—where else—Miami. But Picardi only began the job officially in March, meaning his tenure at the publisher only lasted a brief eight months. Given all the fanfare surrounding his appointment, I have to imagine something went seriously awry. Or Picardi, who did not return my request for comment, landed an otherwise irrefusable job elsewhere. This is disappointing because I liked the direction Playboy was heading under Picardi, reporting on the state of sex, dating, and relationships in this fraught moment—but maybe the loyal fanbase did not.

    Sources indicate that buzzFeed Taps Influential (EXCLUSIVE): On Monday, BuzzFeed named its first chief revenue officer under its new ownership, tapping Chris Poydenis, co-founder of the creator marketing firm Influential, to lead its revenue division. The appointment comes as BuzzFeed attempts an ambitious shift in direction, positioning itself as a source of free, ad-supported television, bundled with the rest of the Allen Media Group portfolio. The decision to name a creator marketing executive as the chief sales lead clearly telegraphs the manner in which BuzzFeed would like to evolve, shifting focus to its creators and video franchise talent. Will it work? The odds are long.

    Sara Kehaulani Goo is president of The Washington Post’s creator network, a latest division that sits outside of the newsroom and makes sponsored short-form video series with independent creators. Goo, formerly the editor in chief of Axios, launched the first show in April, and the network has since released six series in categories ranging from personal finance to career advice.

    Publishers increasingly want to work with creators, but the harder question is why creators would want to work with publishers. In our conversation, Goo and I discussed how The Post’s model works, why its creator content goes through Post fact-checking, and what a media company can offer talent who could go it alone.

    This interview has been edited.

    Sources indicate that mark Stenberg: You specifically left Axios to head up this latest creator division. Can you tell me about the role and how The Post is working with creators?

    It has been revealed that sara Kehaulani Goo: I spent 12 years of my career at The Post as a reporter and editor, so it’s been nice to return in a very different role. The theory is simple: Look at where people spend their time, where they get information, where trust is growing, and where revenue is growing across media. The answer to all of those questions is creators. So, we are working with knowledge creators, people who have built big audiences around their expertise, and treating them as equal editorial and business partners.

    Mark: How does a show actually work?

    Industry observers note that sara: We mostly work with creators who’ve built audiences with short-form video in lifestyle topics like personal finance, health and wellness, and career advice. Then, we develop the shows together and publish them together. Last week, we rolled out Her Next Move with an executive recruiter based in Latest York. She posts a two-minute video to her audience of a million people as a collab with us, so it reaches both audiences. We amplify it on The Post’s social accounts and publish it on our website and app. That show is sponsored by Uber.

    Recent findings suggest that mark: Why would a creator want to work with the Post? Do they share in the revenue?

    In a recent development, sara: I won’t get into the details, but we pay them for their time. It’s similar to a contributor model, though not exactly like freelancing, because they’re entrepreneurs. A lot of them want to focus on the content, which is what journalists want too. We help build the business around them, and we provide distribution and editorial support when they need it.

    Mark: Does their content go through Post fact-checking?

    Recent findings suggest that sara: Yes, through my team. The standards are the same. There’s a lack of consistency in the creator world when it comes to disclosing sponsorships, and to quality in general, and we can bring that. Trust in creators is growing, but people still wonder whether they should trust what they’re watching on Instagram and who paid for it. We can help answer that.

    Mark: It’s early, but how big is this now, and where is it headed?

    In a recent development, sara: This year has been a proof of concept. We’ve done six shows with six creators, across health and wellness, personal finance, travel, career advice, and entertainment. Now we’re deciding which ones to renew, and next year we want to do more always-on content. Brands are very interested, because every brand is thinking about its creator strategy, and finding the right creator takes a lot of effort. We take that headache off their shoulders.

    In a recent development, mark: Creators often relish operating on their own. How do you convince them to work with you?

    Sara: Having led newsrooms, I’ve always seen my job as spotting talent, developing it, and creating an environment where people can do their best work. This is the same. Creators are entrepreneurs, and the platforms give them plenty of ways to make money on their own. But being an entrepreneur isn’t for everybody, at least not at every level. Media companies have always worked with outside experts. The structure just looks different now.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • We’re looking for a Software Engineer to join Supabase’s Interfaces group and help run the backend services behind our developer tools, starting with postgres-meta: the open-source service that runs SQL against customers’ Postgres databases on behalf of our dashboard, our MCP server, AI agents, and other platform tools.
    • It has been revealed that AI agents are the fastest-growing source of postgres-meta’s traffic, and it sits on the path between developers and their data, so when it struggles, people can’t reach their databases from the dashboard or their agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Software Engineer to join Supabase’s Interfaces group and help run the backend services behind our developer tools, starting with postgres-meta: the open-source service that runs SQL against customers’ Postgres databases on behalf of our dashboard, our MCP server, AI agents, and other platform tools. You’ll work closely with the engineers who build those tools, and with our Platform and SRE teams.

    It has been revealed that AI agents are the fastest-growing source of postgres-meta’s traffic, and it sits on the path between developers and their data, so when it struggles, people can’t reach their databases from the dashboard or their agents. The team’s first priority is making it reliable, observable, and fair between tenants at agent scale, and helping redesign it for that scale without breaking the tools that depend on it. Depending on your experience, you’ll own major parts of that work or lead it. Alongside it, the team builds the backend services that give every branch of a project the configuration and secrets it needs.

    We want to be upfront: this role carries real operational load. Our on-call process and rotation are fresh and need a lot of maturing, and you’ll help build them into something sustainable from your first weeks. You’ll be on call for services on the critical path, and incidents come before planned work. Platform teams run the infrastructure underneath; you’ll own the services themselves, from their code to how they behave in production. It’s ideal for someone who enjoys that kind of ownership, thrives in async, fast-paced environments, and stays calm when the root cause turns out to be in someone else’s system.

    Industry observers note that help mature the team’s on-call from your first weeks: grow the rotation to cover every service the team runs, write runbooks, and agree when to declare an incident. Then build it, with our embedded SRE, into a sustainable follow-the-sun rotation as the team grows.

    Set SLOs with the teams that call the service, and build the observability to hold them: metrics per tenant and per caller, alerts that catch failures wherever they start, and logs you can search across regions.

    Make deploys routine with canary and staged rollouts, so dependency and security upgrades stop being risky.

    Redesign how the service works with Postgres at scale: reusing connections, limiting or streaming large results, and isolating and rate-limiting tenants, so no single caller, human or agent, can degrade it for everyone else.

    Help decide the service’s long-term architecture with our Platform teams, then evolve it without breaking the callers that depend on it.

    Write down and agree the service’s contract with its callers, including the dashboard, MCP and AI, and platform workers: how transactions, multi-statement queries, timeouts, and errors behave.

    Work through incidents with the networking, Kubernetes, pooler, and control-plane teams when a problem on the path to customers’ databases starts in their systems.

    Build backend services for code-first workflows, starting with delivering each branch’s configuration and secrets to the services that need them.

    Make small changes directly in the CLI, dashboard, or docs when a capability needs them, with the owning team reviewing.

    Review code and designs, mentor other engineers, and grow into leading the team’s technical direction.

    Have 5+ years of experience as a software engineer, most of it building and running backend services in production.

    Have run a high-traffic, multi-tenant service in production: been on call for it, worked incidents through to resolution, and followed through on postmortems.

    Write strong TypeScript, and work confidently in a large Node.js backend codebase.

    Understand Postgres from the client side: connection management and pooling, transactions, statement timeouts and cancellation, and large result sets.

    Have built observability for a service you owned (metrics, tracing, logs, and alerts tied to SLOs), and used it to debug problems that span proxies, load balancers, or Kubernetes.

    Have kept a service healthy under load with patterns such as rate limiting, timeouts, memory limits, and graceful degradation.

    Have shipped changes to a live service safely, with canaries, staged rollouts, feature flags, or fast rollback.

    Work calmly and constructively with other teams during incidents, including when the root cause is in a system you don’t own.

    Communicate clearly in writing, from design docs to postmortems, thrive in async, globally distributed teams, and make progress when the path isn’t fully defined.

    Nice to have, roughly in order of how much they’d help:.

    Have rebuilt or migrated a live, high-traffic service without breaking its callers, using techniques such as shadow traffic, contract tests, or incremental replacement.

    Have led the design of reliability work, such as tenant isolation, load shedding, or a staged-deploy pipeline, or set technical direction that other engineers built on.

    Have built or operated a database proxy or connection pooler (such as PgBouncer, Supavisor, or pgcat), or an API gateway such as Envoy.

    Have secured a service that runs SQL on its callers’ behalf: handling credentials safely, and limiting how much damage any one caller can do.

    Production experience in a second backend language, such as Elixir or Go.

    Experience with a secrets manager or key management service, such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS KMS.

    Familiarity with Supabase, or with how AI agents use databases through tools like MCP.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Industry observers note that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Sources indicate that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are key to us.

    Recent findings suggest that once a year, the entire organization gathers in a upcoming city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    According to recent reports, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    According to recent reports, at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    According to recent reports, atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid. Our mission is to tear down barriers between people in crisis and the aid they deserve. In the last six years, we’ve become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We also help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    According to recent reports, so far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews. And we’re just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, Google Ventures, and True Ventures, and we’re on our way to creating a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Recent findings suggest that in the next two years, we aim to help over 250,000 Americans get access to life-changing benefits. Much of that help reaches people through our Lawyer Network: our network of vetted partner law firms that represent clients alongside Atticus. The Lawyer Network (LN) team, led by Erin Casale, is the bridge between Atticus and those firms, and our job is to improve their ability to serve clients and help them grow.

    We're hiring a Senior Account Manager to own our largest partner firms. You'll carry a deliberately small book of high-volume firms (roughly 10) and act as an extension of their team: diagnosing where and why they lose cases, coaching them on operations and legal execution, and getting even the most technophobic firm to adopt new Atticus tools.

    The ideal candidate has spent years making small business customers measurably better at what they do through a mix of operations and tech, and wants to do that work somewhere it changes lives.

    Recent findings suggest that make firms better. Own our enterprise-tier partner firms and improve their capacity, conversion rates, and win rates. Find best practices in firm operations and Social Security Disability legal execution, spread them across the network, and coach them relentlessly.

    Industry observers note that drive technology adoption. Get every firm, including folks who are tech-hesitant, using new Atticus features well. That means making the case for the value (think: sales motion but the product is free), building and implementing change management plans, and running training and support.

    Industry observers note that know your firms from the inside. Build relationships beyond the managing attorney, down to intake, case development, and operations leads. Understand a firm well enough to help with hiring, software, and staffing decisions, not just Atticus problems.

    Be the voice of firms inside Atticus. Bring what you learn back to Product, Customer Experience, and Operations so we serve firms better and learn from their experience.

    Sources indicate that deliver hard news well. Hold firms to clear performance standards and push back on attorneys—even those with decades of experience in the field—with finesse and confidence. If needed, cut ties gracefully.

    Sources indicate that shape how the team works. Own strategic projects end to end, from scoping the question and gathering data to sharing recommendations with leadership and rolling out what works across the network.

    5+ years in Account Management, Customer Success, Partnerships, or a similar role serving small businesses, where your mandate was improving your accounts' performance (not just retention).

    A track record of driving product adoption in a tech or tech-adjacent setting.

    You read data comfortably, spot trends before results move, and show up with both a diagnosis and a plan.

    You're persuasive in conversation and in writing, and you'd rather pick up the phone (or get on a plane) than send another email.

    You're outgoing and build trust quickly, with colleagues and with skeptical partners alike.

    Adaptable: resourceful and steady when priorities shift.

    You pick up upcoming tools fast, from cloud software to building a clean deck.

    It has been revealed that we covered above why this job might be for you, and think it’s equally important to tell you why it might not be for you. You won’t enjoy this job very much if:.

    You prefer a large book of light-touch accounts over depth with a few.

    You want a predictable playbook.

    You get frustrated when projects and priorities change quickly (we obviously try to limit this, but are a quickly-growing firm and it does still happen).

    It has been revealed that the role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup that doubles as a B-corp social enterprise. Our team is still small enough for you to have an outsized impact on how we operate and how our firms grow.

    We offer competitive pay, including equity, and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employee and family premiums covered.

    15 vacation days and ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    According to recent reports, we anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $110,000 and $130,000, in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as the candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    This job is fully remote and we're committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the organization dime) as needed to be with your colleagues, usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather. You'll also visit partner firms in-person occasionally. Overall, expect to travel up to monthly between internal get togethers and firm visits.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Internal IT Manager owns the Service Desk and the Corporate Systems that run the business, and builds the AI driven workflows that connect them. You run the team and you also build: you design the automations, ship the integrations, and show the team how it is done. You set priorities, coach each person, and build alongside them.

    In a recent development, you lead a small, hands on team that keeps the company running and builds toward AI Native. The team shares one queue, reviews metrics, and brings automation ideas to the company.

    ServiceDesk and ticketing• Run the ServiceDesk across onboarding, offboarding, access requests, hardware and software support.• Own the ticketing platform: queues, categories, SLAs, escalation paths, and reporting.• Cut ticket volume through self service, knowledge base content, and AI assisted triage and resolution.Asset management• Maintain one accurate inventory of hardware, software licenses, and SaaS subscriptions.• Manage the full asset lifecycle: procurement, provisioning, tracking, refresh, and secure disposal.• Reconcile licenses against real usage to remove waste before each renewal.Corporate systems• Administer the core business stack: identity and SSO (Okta), device management (Iru), collaboration tools, and the systems used by People, Sales, Legal, and Finance.• Keep systems secure, documented, and available, with clear owners and change control.• Evaluate new tools and retire those that no longer earn their cost.Corporate contracts and vendors• Manage IT vendor relationships, renewals, and negotiations.• Maintain a contract register with owners, terms, renewal dates, and spend.• Work with Legal and Finance on reviews, security questionnaires, and budget forecasts.

    AI and enterprise workflowsYou treat AI as a core tool for running IT, and you build with it yourself.• Design and ship automated workflows for onboarding, offboarding, access provisioning, approvals, and renewals.• Integrate systems through APIs, webhooks, and iPaaS tools so data moves between ticketing, identity, HR, CRM, finance, and contract platforms without manual steps.• Deploy AI agents and assistants for ticket triage, knowledge search, request fulfillment, and employee support.• Write scripts and light code (Python, JavaScript, PowerShell) when a ready made tool falls short.• Set guardrails for AI use: data handling, access scope, review steps, and audit trails, agreed with Legal and Security.• Measure each automation by hours saved, errors avoided, and adoption, then improve or retire it.

    • 5+ years in IT operations, with 2+ years leading a IT Operations or internal IT team.• Hands on experience administering corporate systems: identity and SSO (Okta), MDM, Google Workspace, and SaaS management.• Working knowledge of vendor contracts, renewals, and procurement.• Demonstrated delivery of automations and integrations using APIs, webhooks, and automation tools such as Zapier, or n8n.• Practical experience applying AI tools to IT work: agents, assistants, and workflow automation.• Scripting ability in Python, Bash, or PowerShell.• Strong written and spoken communication, with the ability to work with Legal, People, Sales, and Finance.• Sound judgment on security, privacy, and compliance basics.

    Please note that this role may evolve as our business needs change, so we appreciate your flexibility and adaptability.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off and National Holidays: Enjoy 20 PTO days yearly and the National Holidays for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Industry observers note that clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS manufacturer, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

    Please note: This position is offered on a contractor basis. Applicants must have the necessary documentation and authorization to work in the country where the job is located. Clutch cannot provide sponsorship or assist with obtaining work permits for this role.A Note About AI at ClutchWe love AI. If you join Clutch, we hope you'll bring the same enthusiasm for exploring how AI can amplify impact, productivity, and innovation.That stated, during the interview process, we want to hear your thoughts.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
    • It has been revealed that we're looking for a Senior People Business Partner for our GTM org.
    • You build the kind of relationships where leaders and individual contributors bring you the hard stuff while there's still time to proactively do something about it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    It has been revealed that we're looking for a Senior People Business Partner for our GTM org. You don't need to be the deep expert in every corner, but you're dangerous enough across all of it to move fast and recognize when something deserves more attention than you can give it right now. You also know when to slow down and when to raise the harder question early.

    You build the kind of relationships where leaders and individual contributors bring you the hard stuff while there's still time to proactively do something about it. You're approachable, direct, and willing to push back when something doesn't make sense. You don't need every answer, but you know how to ask good questions, work through messy situations, and help leaders make better decisions.

    You'll partner with leaders across Sales, Marketing, and the rest of our revenue organization as they build and grow their teams, and you'll work closely with our VP of People and the broader People team to build scalable, intentional People programs that enable folks to do their best work.

    You'll thrive as a People Business Partner if you:.

    Take the time to understand the business just as much as the people side.

    Have worked in enough different environments to have a real sense of what good looks like, and hold yourself to it.

    Stay steady when a sales org is moving fast: quota changes, reorgs, and rapid hiring don't rattle you.

    Are direct with people, including when it's uncomfortable—feedback doesn't get softened into confusion, and people still trust you after.

    Assess risk quickly—not just what could go wrong, but what's actually likely to and how much it matters.

    Know when to escalate and when to just decide; you bring a recommendation, not just a problem, and you know which things (comp exceptions, anything legal, changes to established policy) always get a second set of eyes.

    As a People Business Partner at LiveKit, you will:.

    Own performance management, manager coaching, org design, and headcount planning as the primary People partner for Sales, Marketing, and our broader Revenue organization, including pre- and post-sales teams.

    Navigate complex situations and help the org grow without breaking, including pushing back on adding layers or headcount before the case is made.

    Partner with our GTM Talent Partner on hiring plans, role scoping, and ramp so headcount decisions are made with the full picture.

    Work as one team with the other People Business Partners (EPD and G&A) so leaders get a consistent partnership experience.

    Work directly with the VP of People and larger People and Talent team to design, build, and operationalize People programs across all COEs.

    Own end-to-end delivery of programs and projects, from strategy to rollout to iteration.

    Make our work repeatable: documented, handoff-ready, and not dependent on anyone being a hero.

    Experience as a People Business Partner (or equivalent) supporting Sales and other revenue-generating teams: performance management against quota and ramp, comp blueprint changes, rev org reorgs, and coaching sales managers.

    Think from first principles and know when to ask for help.

    A clear, direct communicator who can challenge strong personalities while maintaining trust.

    Confident in what you know and what you don't—able to respond decisively even without full information.

    Comfortable in ambiguity, with strong relationship-building instincts and data-informed decision-making.

    Personable, approachable, and comfortable working with leaders and ICs at all levels.

    Understand how hiring, talent development, and organizational decisions impact a sales team's success.

    Experience with global HR, leaves of absence, or benefits administration.

    Direct experience building or significantly iterating programs across multiple People COEs.

    Experience using AI tools to improve how you work, with good judgment about when and how to use them.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Work alongside world-class people at one of the most vital AI infrastructure companies being built right now.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • Creators use Kit's first-party apps and integrations to connect Kit to the rest of their business.
    • You'll be the first engineer on the Apps squad.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Creators use Kit's first-party apps and integrations to connect Kit to the rest of their business. Today we build and maintain these apps by hand, with help from an agency partner. That doesn't scale. We're looking for a Senior Software Engineer II to own app delivery and maintenance end to end, so a small team can support creators of every size.

    You'll be the first engineer on the Apps squad. Your focus is shipping high quality apps at a high pace, and maintaining them to an industry-best standard. To get there, you'll take a systems-level view and build on Kit's coding agent. You'll work closely with our AI Developer Experience squad, which builds the coding agent. You'll own the creator experience of every app you build, and you're free to improve Kit's platform when that makes those apps better.

    This is a full-time IC role for an AI-first, product-minded, full-stack engineer who has shipped agent workflows to production and judges them by reliable outcomes, not lines of code. You combine technical depth with leadership and extreme ownership. You take input from Partnerships, Product, and Design to help shape the "what," and you own the "how." You thrive in ambiguity, take initiative without waiting for permission, and elevate everyone around you through your generosity and optimism.

    It has been revealed that we're excited about first-party apps because they let creators do more with Kit than Kit does on its own. Our own apps should just work, and set the bar for every app built on Kit.

    You'll report to John Bohannon, Senior Engineering Manager for the Ecosystem and Apps squads. You'll collaborate closely with a Partnerships Manager, Product Manager, Product Designer, and engineers on the Ecosystem squad. You'll also work closely with our AI Developer Experience squad on Kit's coding agent, and with a contractor who helps maintain our apps.

    It has been revealed that the Apps squad works as a sibling to Ecosystem. You'll set its rhythms, collaborate with our Partnerships Manager on which apps to build next, and join Ecosystem's cycle planning.

    A peer onboarding buddy will help you learn our systems and codebase, and you'll have engineers across Kit for support and mentorship.

    Industry observers note that first Week: Set up your local environment and merge your first production code. Meet the team through Get To Know You's. Start the app handover with the contractor who maintains them today. Watch the recorded app walkthroughs and read the runbooks for our most-used apps.

    Sources indicate that first Month: Audit our first-party apps and integrations, starting with the apps that need the most maintenance. Measure what each app costs to maintain, including partner app reviews like those at Google, Meta, and Shopify. Learn how Kit's API, OAuth, and App Store support creators from small to large. Fix bugs and support escalations in the apps you now own. Learn how Kit's coding agent works with the AI Developer Experience squad.

    First Three Months: Adapt Kit's coding agent to build your first apps and maintain existing ones. Give it the context, guardrails, and evals it needs. Turn what you learn into shared pieces every app can use, like a reusable load test, infrastructure automation, and app manifests. Write runbooks that let others work on any app. Drive each app's maintenance toward zero human time with the coding agent.

    According to recent reports, first Six Months: Ship newly introduced apps at a steady pace. Take over the rest of the app catalog and apply the coding agent to its maintenance. Show that one engineer with agents can maintain many apps at high quality. Define the metrics and dashboards for agent-built apps: rolls out, reliability, time to fix, and revenue impact. Share how agents build and maintain our apps, for example in a Lunch & Learn.

    Sources indicate that first Year: Kit ships more high-quality apps, faster, and the coding agent handles more of the routine builds and fixes, with you steering the system. The legacy integration model is retired. You use catalog metrics to recommend where the Apps squad invests next. You and the AI Developer Experience squad improve the coding agent together, so other Kit engineers benefit too.

    Industry observers note that expert in agentic AI development. You've built agent workflows that ship and maintain production code, with evals, guardrails, and human review.

    Industry observers note that strong in APIs, including OAuth, webhooks, and integrations with third-party platforms. Fluent in Ruby on Rails, or able to ramp into it fast. Full-stack, with React where an app needs it.

    Ship well-tested, performant, accessible code, whether you or an agent writes it. Set the quality bar and build the tests, evals, and reviews that hold agents to it.

    Set up dashboards, alerts, and load tests that find problems across many apps early.

    Measure each app's maintenance cost, and make the team's open capacity for new apps easy to see.

    Communicate clearly across Engineering, Product, Design, and Partnerships.

    Align others on goals, trade-offs, and success criteria without formal authority.

    Led a major cross-team initiative from ambiguous requirements to delivery, partnering with senior leaders across functions, with measurable business impact.

    Built agents or tools that measurably improved how a team ships software, not only how much code it writes.

    Took ownership of a codebase someone else built, with thin documentation, and made it maintainable.

    Independently managed a large project, such as a migration or deprecation that required customers or partners to move.

    Create leverage, not only features. Invest in reusable systems that make your team and others faster.

    Judge AI work by outcomes, like introduces and reliability, not by the volume of code or PRs. Share what works and what the risks are.

    Own everything you and your agents produce, from code to PR descriptions. Know the details well enough to stand behind every line, and don't leave reviewers or readers to do the work.

    Lead work without waiting for a formal role or permission.

    Make reversible product decisions on your own, and know when to pull in cross-functional stakeholders like Product, Design, Partnerships, and Support.

    Break big, ambiguous problems into steps that you and others can deliver.

    Write docs that let others work on any app, so the work doesn't depend on one person.

    Put creator outcomes ahead of features.

    Industry observers note that share work in progress and the reasons behind trade-offs. Give and ask for direct feedback.

    You will stand out if you have:.

    Built AI tools that other developers use, such as MCP servers, agent skills, or eval suites.

    Built integrations with creator-economy platforms.

    Directed the work of contractors or an agency partner.

    Shared your work through talks, blog posts, or open-source contributions.

    Needing established processes, full consensus, or permission before you move forward.

    Wanting a large team of engineering peers on your own team from day one.

    Preferring to stay heads-down in code over shaping what to build with Partnerships, Product, and Design.

    Preferring greenfield work over inheriting and improving legacy code.

    Building each app by hand when a shared system could serve many.

    Measuring AI success by code volume instead of shipped, reliable apps.

    Avoiding direct feedback, whether giving or receiving it.

    According to recent reports, we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Recent findings suggest that kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level P4 ($186,000/year). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance prepares through Aetna.

    $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    Sources indicate that we usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    Phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    Technical execution and leadership/collaboration interview (60 min).

    In a recent development, we’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    We value diversity in all of its forms. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • According to recent reports, we’re looking for a Head of M&A to join our Corporate Development team and help build M&A from scratch.
    • This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    According to recent reports, we’re looking for a Head of M&A to join our Corporate Development team and help build M&A from scratch. You’ll work closely with product, engineering, finance, legal, as well as founders we might acquire, helping us build a world class M&A team.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Map the markets and targets that matter to Supabase's roadmap, and keep the map current.

    Decide build vs buy each quarter for key product areas, together with Product and Engineering.

    Build relationships with founders early, and convert the ones we want.

    Write the case for, price, and negotiate deals, from valuation model to term sheet to close.

    Run diligence and integration end to end alongside Engineering, People, Finance, and Legal.

    Set and own integration milestones, and track every deal against the reason we did it.

    Build automation for target discovery, relationship tracking, and diligence.

    Build the Supabase M&A muscle, and improve it after every deal.

    Note: Supabase is here to scale revenue, not headcount. You should be as comfortable as a IC as a cross functional leader, and want to build the system, not the org chart.

    Have 7+ years of experience in M&A.

    Are comfortable in highly technical domains.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Have experience in async or globally distributed teams.

    Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Industry observers note that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    In a recent development, once a year, the entire firm gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Sources indicate that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Sources indicate that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.
